title: Lagged wallet event channel silently drops Reorg events, leaving demoted txids unqueued
comment: In `drain_wallet_events`, a `TryRecvError::Lagged(n)` continues the loop and processes subsequent messages, but the lagged messages (which may include `Reorg` events) are permanently lost. The wallet event broadcast channel capacity is whatever the `WalletInterface` implementation provides — in `MockWallet` it is 16. During rapid block syncing or a sequence of reorgs, if `drain_wallet_events` (called every tick) falls behind, a `Reorg` event can be evicted from the ring buffer before it is consumed. The consequence is that `demoted_txids` from the missed `Reorg` are never enqueued in `pending_rebroadcast`, and the user's demoted transactions are silently abandoned without any UI notification. A tracing warning is emitted, but no recovery attempt is made. Consider subscribing to the wallet's event channel with a larger capacity, or adding a reconciliation path that re-queries the wallet's pending-reorg state after a lag is detected.
judgeNotes: Merged findings 3 and 5 — same issue, two reviewers. Real data-loss path: a lagged broadcast subscription permanently drops Reorg events, leaving demoted txids unqueued with no recovery. Impact: High (silent abandonment of user txs), Likelihood: Possible (requires lag under load with default capacity) → warning.
label: false

title: BIP157 filter-header integrity check path is completely untested
comment: The block that calls `load_filter_headers(start..tip + 1)` and truncates both filter headers and filters on a read error has no test at all. A false positive (spurious truncation of valid data) silently discards correct sync progress; a false negative (corruption that happens to decode without error) leaves the client with a corrupt filter-header chain that can cause incorrect filter matching. A test should write a full set of filter headers, overwrite part of a segment file with garbage bytes, reopen the storages, run `check_and_repair_consistency`, and assert both filter headers and filters are truncated back to `block_tip`.
judgeNotes: Impact: Medium-High (corruption recovery code untested), Likelihood: Possible. Real coverage concern but the code itself is plausibly correct; suggestion fits low-noise bar.

title: Integration test races against QRInfo response when asserting engine state after ChainReorg
comment: After `wait_for_chain_reorg_event` returns, the test immediately reads the engine and asserts `highest <= fork_height`. The `ChainReorg` event is broadcast after `rewind_to_height` completes — at which point the QRInfo request is already in flight on the network. In a fast-local-loopback regtest environment, the dashd response could arrive and be processed by the SPV client between the event broadcast and the engine lock acquisition, causing the engine to already have re-populated lists above `fork_height` and the assertion to fail spuriously. The window is narrow in practice (network RTT vs. in-process assertion), but the test infrastructure does nothing to prevent it. Fix by observing engine state from within the `rewind_to_height` path itself (e.g., via a dedicated event) rather than polling after the reorg event, or by asserting only the post-rewind `MasternodeStateUpdated` properties.
judgeNotes: Merged findings 3, 6, 9, and 15 — four reviewers independently flagged this race. The intermediate engine assertion runs after the ChainReorg broadcast but with no synchronization barrier ensuring rewind_to_height has acquired/released the write lock and that no QRInfo response has been applied. Impact: Medium (test flake, not production bug), Likelihood: Possible (timing-dependent on fast regtest loopback) → warning. Strong consensus among reviewers.

title: Generation check drops valid pre-fork blocks, forcing unnecessary re-downloads
comment: The generation stamp is written once per `send_pending_with_generation` call. Every block requested before the generation bump — including blocks at heights strictly ≤ `fork_height` whose headers are unchanged by the reorg — carries the old generation and is silently dropped by the `req_gen != current_gen` guard. This is safe (BlocksManager resets on `ChainReorg` and those blocks will be re-requested after the full filter re-sync), but it adds a redundant full-pipeline download cycle even for the portion of the chain below the fork. If blocks below the fork arrive after the pipeline reset they fall through to the `receive_block` path harmlessly; it is only the in-flight ones at reorg time that are wasted. A height-aware guard (`height > fork_height`) would recover those blocks without complicating the cascade.
judgeNotes: Reviewer explicitly notes this is safe — BlocksManager resets and re-requests after the cascade. Impact is just an extra download cycle, which is acceptable for an infrequent event like reorg. Optimisation, not a correctness bug.
label: false

title: ForkCandidate::tip_hash panics on empty headers without construction-site enforcement
judgeNotes: Merged findings 6 and 14. The invariant is documented and enforced at construction (fork buffer guarantees non-empty candidates). title: `best_chainlock_height()` uses 0 as "no chainlock" sentinel, shadowing height 0
comment: The `AtomicU32` is initialised to 0 and the accessor maps 0 → `None`. This conflates "no chainlock observed" with "chainlock issued at genesis height 0". While a height-0 chainlock is semantically implausible today, if one is ever persisted and restored via `ChainLockManager::new`, the `chainlock_height.store(cl.block_height, …)` call will write 0, and `best_chainlock_height()` will return `None`, silently ignoring the persisted value and removing the cascade floor. The `AtomicU32`-based API also makes it impossible to distinguish these two states for callers. Changing to a sentinel of `u32::MAX` (or accepting a marginal allocation with `Arc<Mutex<Option<u32>>>`) removes the ambiguity without changing the hot-path read cost.
judgeNotes: A height-0 chainlock is implausible in practice (genesis blocks aren't chainlocked). The ambiguity is real but the failure mode requires a scenario that does not occur. Sentinel cleanup is reasonable code hygiene.
label: false

title: `try_evict_for_incoming` removes peer from pool but leaves reader task and TCP connection running

title: pending_fork_candidate is a single slot: rapid second fork silently drops the first candidate
comment: ingest_fork always overwrites self.pending_fork_candidate with the latest winning branch without checking whether the slot is already occupied. If two different fork branches both beat the active chain and ingest_fork fires twice before the phase-3 coordinator calls take_pending_fork_candidate(), the first candidate is silently dropped from the slot (it has already been removed from the fork_buffer by take_winning_candidate). The second candidate wins the slot and the first is permanently lost. During a contested multi-branch reorg scenario this means the heavier fork could be discarded in favour of the most-recently-processed winner. The field should be a VecDeque or the caller should check for an occupied slot before overwriting.
judgeNotes: Impact: Medium (heavier fork could be discarded in favor of newer one), Likelihood: Unlikely (requires two competing winning forks before Phase 3 drains). Merged with finding 14 — same single-slot overwrite issue. Author should at minimum log when overwriting; queue is open to discussion. Downgraded because Phase 3 promotion isn't wired up yet so impact today is bounded.

title: `ForkBuffer::ingest` missing future-timestamp upper-bound check
comment: The ingest loop enforces MTP (lower timestamp bound) but not dashd's `MAX_FUTURE_BLOCK_TIME` upper bound. On testnet/devnet (`allow_min_difficulty_blocks = true`), a peer can set `header.time` arbitrarily far in the future: this passes the MTP check, then triggers the `gap > 2h` branch in the newly-added `min_difficulty_bits`, returning `pow_limit` difficulty. A single malicious peer can therefore fill its 16-branch per-peer quota with one easy-PoW header per branch at minimal cost. The TTL mechanism bounds the window but the PR summary claims full `ContextualCheckBlockHeader` equivalence — the missing upper timestamp check makes that incomplete. Add a caller-supplied `now: u32` parameter and reject headers where `header.time > now + MAX_FUTURE_BLOCK_TIME`; on mainnet this is unnecessary but costs nothing to check.
judgeNotes: Single reviewer. On mainnet DGW already constrains bits; the testnet/devnet min-difficulty bypass is real but bounded by TTL and per-peer branch cap. Worth noting but not a behavioral blocker for this PR.

title: Breaking trait change: four public traits gain required methods with no default implementations
comment:
`truncate_above` is added as a required `async fn` to `BlockHeaderStorage`, `FilterHeaderStorage`, `FilterStorage`, and `BlockStorage` without a default implementation. Any downstream crate — or any in-tree mock — that implements one of these traits will fail to compile immediately after merging. The test `MockHeaderStorage` in `sync/masternodes/sync_manager.rs` demonstrates the impact: it already needed a stub added. Providing a default that returns `Err(StorageError::NotSupported(...))` or `unimplemented!()` would keep existing implementors compiling while making the gap visible at runtime rather than compile time. Given the 0.x.x API stability policy this is expected, but the change should be called out in release notes.

<details>
<summary>Suggested fix</summary>

````suggestion
Add a default body so existing implementors continue to compile:
```rust
async fn truncate_above(&mut self, _target_height: u32) -> StorageResult<()> {
    Err(StorageError::WriteFailed("truncate_above not implemented".into()))
}
```
````
</details>
label: false

title: Cross-storage truncation is non-atomic and not surfaced on StorageManager
comment:
`DiskStorageManager` implements `truncate_above` separately for each storage type via four independent write locks. A caller performing a reorg must acquire and truncate `block_headers`, `filter_headers`, `filters`, and `blocks` in sequence. If any step fails mid-way, the remaining storages are left at a higher tip than `block_headers`, producing inconsistent state: the SPV client may trust filter headers or filters that correspond to orphaned block headers. The `StorageManager` supertrait does not expose a coordinated `truncate_above`, so there is no single call-site that can be made atomic even with a future fix. Phase 3 guards should route through a single coordinated entry point rather than calling each storage independently.

<details>
<summary>Suggested fix</summary>

````suggestion
Add a coordinated method to `StorageManager`:
```rust
async fn truncate_above(&mut self, target_height: u32) -> StorageResult<()>;
```
Implement it in `DiskStorageManager` to truncate all four sub-storages in order, returning the first error without proceeding further. Document the expected compensation strategy (e.g., full re-sync) if any step fails. This is a prerequisite for Phase 3 rather than Phase 1, but the interface design decision should be locked in now to avoid a second breaking change.
````
</details>
label: false

title: Deserialize rebuilds spent_outpoints from inactive transactions
comment:
The custom `Deserialize` impl rebuilds `spent_outpoints` by collecting every transaction input across all recorded transactions, with no filter for `Conflicted` or `Abandoned` records. But `release_inactive_utxos` explicitly removes those inputs from `spent_outpoints` when a transition to inactive occurs. After a serialize/deserialize round-trip, inactive transactions' inputs are incorrectly re-inserted into `spent_outpoints`, making those outpoints appear "spent" again. Any UTXO that should have been freed by the conflict/abandonment will be treated as still consumed, producing incorrect balance and potentially blocking re-spend of the same coins in a future transaction.

<details>
<summary>Suggested fix</summary>

```suggestion
let spent_outpoints = helper
    .keys
    .transactions()
    .values()
    .filter(|record| !record.context.is_inactive())  // exclude Conflicted/Abandoned
    .flat_map(|record| &record.transaction.input)
    .map(|input| input.previous_output)
    .collect();
```
</details>
judgeNotes: Impact: High (silent incorrect balance / blocked re-spend after reload), Likelihood: Certain on any persist→reload after a Conflicted/Abandoned transition. Two reviewers independently identified this (findings 1 and 8); the fix is a one-line filter. Merged finding 8 here.
label: real

title: `SegmentCache::clear_all` misses on-disk-only segments, making the repair non-durable

On restart, load_or_new rediscovers the surviving files and the repair fires again — multiple reviewers (4 of 4) flagged this. title: Mutable action tags on a privileged workflow
comment:
All three actions use mutable version tags (`actions/checkout@v7`, `actions/setup-node@v7`, `manki-review/manki@v6`) in a workflow that holds `id-token: write`, `pull-requests: write`, and `issues: write` permissions. If any of these tags are silently re-pointed to a compromised release, the malicious code runs with those permissions and has access to `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`. The old workflow had the same gap with `@​v4`/`@​v5`, but the diff introduces three new unpinned references. For a cryptocurrency library, pinning actions to their full commit SHA (with the tag in a comment) is standard supply-chain hygiene.

<details>
<summary>Suggested fix</summary>

```suggestion
- uses: actions/checkout@<sha-of-v7>  # v7
- uses: actions/setup-node@<sha-of-v7>  # v7
  with:
    node-version: '24'
- name: Manki Review
  uses: manki-review/manki@<sha-of-v6>  # v6
  with:
    claude_code_oauth_token: ${{ secrets.CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN }}

Caveat: each SHA must be verified against the signed tag at upgrade time, and kept in sync when the action is updated.
```
</details>
judgeNotes: Impact: High (supply-chain compromise could exfiltrate CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN), Likelihood: Unlikely (requires upstream tag repoint). Pinning to SHAs is best practice for a crypto repo, but the old config had the same pattern — this PR doesn't regress posture, just updates versions. Downgraded from warning to suggestion since it's a pre-existing hygiene issue, not introduced by this PR.
label: real

title: Broadcast RecvError::Lagged silently treated as fatal in event-waiter helpers
comment:
Both helper functions map `Err(err)` — which includes `broadcast::error::RecvError::Lagged(n)` — to a generic `panic!("...channel error...")`. After a lag the receiver's internal cursor has already advanced past the dropped messages, so the target event may have been among them. The current code will either: (a) panic with an opaque message if the target was in the dropped window, or (b) keep looping if the target is still buffered. Distinguishing `Lagged` from a closed channel and logging how many messages were skipped makes CI failures far easier to diagnose. Caveat: handling lag by continuing to receive may still miss the target if it was in the dropped window; in that case the test will time out instead of giving an early error.

<details>
<summary>Suggested fix</summary>

```suggestion
recv = receiver.recv() => match recv {
    Ok(event @ SyncEvent::ChainReorg { fork_height, .. })
        if fork_height == expected_fork_height => return event,
    Ok(_) => continue,
    Err(broadcast::error::RecvError::Lagged(_)) => continue,
    Err(err) => panic!("sync event channel closed waiting for ChainReorg: {}", err),
}
```
</details>
judgeNotes: With a 10k-slot buffer lag is unlikely in practice, and on lag the test would just panic instead of silently passing — diagnostic improvement, not a correctness bug. Merged findings 2 and 5.
label: real

title: pub(super) visibility leak driven by test convenience
comment:
enqueue_demoted_for_rebroadcast was private and is now pub(super) solely to let the test in sync_manager.rs seed pending_rebroadcast state. This creates a coupling from the sibling module's test code to a specific internal mutation method, and it means any production code in the sync/mempool parent module could now call it directly, bypassing the normal channel-driven path. The test in manager.rs (test_input_conflict_via_channel_evicts_rebroadcast) demonstrates the right approach: seed state by sending a WalletEvent::Reorg through the broadcast channel and calling drain_wallet_events(), which exercises the real code path. The test_block_processed_removes_confirmed_txids test in sync_manager.rs could do the same instead of calling enqueue_demoted_for_rebroadcast directly, allowing the method to remain private.

<details>
<summary>Suggested fix</summary>

```suggestion
// In manager.rs — conditional visibility so it doesn't appear in production builds:
#[cfg(test)]
pub(super) async fn enqueue_demoted_for_rebroadcast(
    &mut self,
    wallet_id: WalletId,
    demoted_txids: &[Txid],
) { ... }
```
</details>

title: release_inactive_utxos does not restore inputs consumed by the now-inactive transaction
comment:
When a spending transaction transitions to Conflicted or Abandoned, `release_inactive_utxos` removes the inactive tx's own outputs and clears its input references from `spent_outpoints`, but it does not re-insert the UTXOs that the inactive tx consumed. For example: tx A funds the wallet (UTXO A created), tx B spends UTXO A (UTXO A removed from set), then B goes conflicted — after the call, UTXO A remains absent and the balance shows zero instead of the original funded amount. The doc comment acknowledges this is 'the caller's responsibility', but neither `confirm_transaction` nor `record_transaction` implements it. Until #145 provides the rewind logic, wallets with spend chains that include a conflicted/abandoned transaction will silently report incorrect balances.

<details>
<summary>Suggested fix</summary>

```suggestion
No fix here — this is acknowledged as deferred to #145. At minimum, add a debug assertion or a doc note that callers must restore the predecessor UTXOs before calling update_balance(), so the invariant violation is visible during development.
```
</details>
judgeNotes: Impact: High (incorrect balance for spend chains), Likelihood: Probable once a spending tx is marked inactive. Two reviewers flagged it (findings 3 and 7); explicitly deferred to #145 but the doc-only contract is fragile. Merged finding 7 here.
